newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan dollar seen escaping Asia currency woes.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan dollar seen escaping Asia currency woes.

text.p: Despite clear speculative nibbles by offshore investors this week, Taipei analysts say Taiwan's battle-tested currency is unlikely to be the next Asian domino to fall after the Thai baht and Philippine peso.

They say Taiwan's powerful central bank, backed by the world's third largest foreign exchange reserves and a muscular, developed economy, was unlikely to be forced into the kind of exchange rate capitulation accepted by Manila's central bank.

"Taiwan's central bank is much more powerful than the Philippine central bank, and Taiwan's economy is much better, so the bottom line is the central bank simply has better control," said a dealer from a foreign bank.
In the face of intense offshore speculative pressure, the Philippines caved in and allowed the peso to plunge by around 11.5 percent against the dollar before trading was suspended.
The Thai baht, hit by a shock de facto devaluation in early July after the Thai central bank gave in to speculators, also slumped anew on Friday as the peso plunge sparked new jitters.
Regional dealers have been looking over their shoulders wondering which currency might come under attack next.
Offshore speculators turned their attentions to the Taiwan dollar on Monday and early Tuesday, testing the central bank's resolve through buying of non-delivery forwards.

But their foray was short-lived as the central bank sprang into action. The recently depreciating Taiwan dollar slid to eight-year lows on Tuesday and Wednesday, but responded to subtle but firm intervention to rebound sharply on Thursday.
The Taiwan dollar was slightly softer at 27.876 to the dollar at 0700 GMT compared with 27.855 at the close on Thursday, but dealers said its easing was unrelated to the peso.
Dealers say the central bank has been tolerating a slow depreciation dating back to early 1997, but will not allow disruptive volatility in Taiwan's closely monitored forex market.
Unlike the Philippines central bank, Taiwan's has shown itself able to maintain interest rate stability even while warding off speculative pressure on the currency, dealers said.

Taiwan's overnight interbank rate spiked briefly into the low teens in late June as the sizzling stock market sucked liquidity from the money market, but short term rates generally have been low and stable.
The overnight interbank rate stood at 7.427 percent on Friday.
In the Philippines, by contrast, the overnight borrowing rate has soared above 30 percent in the face of the speculative assault, leaving the central bank little room to manoeuvre.
Taiwan's ace is its mountain of forex reserves.

While the Philippine central bank has less than US$12 billion of foreign exchange reserves at its disposal, Taiwan's central bank boasts an imposing war chest of US$90.008 billion -- third largest in the world after Japan and China.
Dealers say the central bank has ample experience deploying those reserves to defend the dollar in the face of adversity.

Taiwan managed to keep its reserves well above US$80 billion even during the March 1996 Taiwan straits missile crisis, when arch rival China menaced the island with massive war games and unarmed ballistic missiles fired into waters near its ports.
Despite a panicked run to U.S. dollars and gold, the central bank doggedly defended the Taiwan currency at its longtime level of T$27.50 to the U.S. dollar.

After two years of slowing growth, Taiwan's economy appears to be enjoying a gathering recovery, with gross domestic product growing an annual 6.83 percent in the first quarter -- compared to just 5.0 percent in the Philippines.

Taiwan's government has given clear signs that it welcomes a modest depreciation of its currency, announcing in mid-1996 -- soon after the missile crisis -- that it was dropping the T$27.5 defence level, a move analysts called a deliberate bid to boost exports.
